chapter_summary:
With your Unity project configured for Android, the next step is to transform your development environment into a deployable application package, specifically an APK (Android Application Package). This APK is the standard format for distributing and installing applications on Android devices. The process involves several key steps, from setting up your device for development to using Unity's build tools and, finally, installing the application.

First, ensure your Android device is ready for development. This means enabling **Developer Options** and **USB Debugging**. To do this, go to your device's `Settings > About phone` and tap on the `Build number` seven times. This will unlock Developer Options. Then, navigate to `Settings > System > Developer options` and toggle on `USB debugging`. This allows your computer to communicate with the device for installing applications and debugging. It's a common mistake to forget this step, leading to your device not being recognized by Unity or `adb`.

Back in Unity, with your Android platform selected in `Build Settings` and XR Plug-in Management configured for ARCore (for AR) or Oculus/OpenXR (for VR like Meta Quest), you're ready to build. Before hitting "Build," let's address application signing. Every Android application must be digitally signed. This is done using a **keystore**. In Unity, under `Edit > Project Settings > Player > Android tab > Publishing Settings`, you'll find options for "Keystore Manager." Here, you can either select an existing keystore or create a new one. When creating a new keystore, you'll define a password for the keystore itself and then create at least one "alias" (a key) within it, also with its own password. Remember these passwords and secure the `.keystore` file; they are irreplaceable for future updates. A common mistake is using a simple password or losing the keystore, which as discussed, prevents future updates.

Once your signing credentials are set, return to `File > Build Settings`. Ensure your desired scenes are checked. You can choose to "Build" (which compiles the project into an APK) or "Build And Run" (which builds and then attempts to install and launch the APK on a connected device). For the first build, "Build" is often preferred so you can locate the APK file and manually install it if needed. When you click "Build," Unity will ask you to choose a location to save the APK. It's a good practice to create a dedicated "Builds" folder in your project directory.

After Unity successfully generates the APK, you can install it on your Android device. If you used "Build And Run" and your device was properly configured, Unity might handle this automatically. Otherwise, you'll use the **Android Debug Bridge (adb)**, a versatile command-line tool. Connect your Android device to your computer via USB. Open your terminal or command prompt and navigate to the directory where your APK is saved. Then, use the command:
```bash
adb install YourAppName.apk
```
If you encounter issues, `adb devices` will list connected devices, helping you verify if your device is recognized. Common errors during installation include "INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS" (if an older version is present, use `adb uninstall com.yourcompany.yourapp` first) or "INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE."

For VR applications targeting devices like Meta Quest, the process is largely similar. You'll use the Oculus XR Plugin or OpenXR Plugin in Unity's XR Plug-in Management. Specific Player Settings for Oculus might include setting the `Color Space` to `Linear` for better visual quality and ensuring `Virtual Reality Supported` is checked (though XR Plug-in Management largely supersedes this). Meta Quest devices also often require sideloading using `adb` or the `SideQuest` desktop application for development builds. When building for Quest, ensure you select the correct target device in the Oculus XR Plugin settings if applicable, and that the `Minimum API Level` is appropriate for the Quest OS version.

Debugging on device is crucial. While Unity's console logs are helpful during development, on-device debugging often requires `adb logcat` to view device logs in real-time.
```bash
adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager
```
This command filters logs for Unity and ActivityManager, providing insights into crashes or runtime errors specific to your application. Remote debugging with Unity's Profiler is also possible, allowing you to monitor performance metrics directly from the device, which we'll cover in a later chapter. Always remember to test your application thoroughly on the target device, as performance and behavior can differ significantly from the Unity Editor.

screens.title: Building and Deploying to Android (ARCore/VR)
screens.subtitle: Turn your Unity project into an installable APK, sign it securely, and test it on Android and Android-based VR headsets.

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn the full path from a Unity project to a working Android application package. We will make sure your phone or headset is ready for development, walk through creating a keystore so your app is signed, and use adb to install and inspect your build. You will see concrete build steps in Unity, the difference between "Build" and "Build And Run," and commands for installing and viewing device logs. I will also show you the special considerations for Android-based VR headsets like the Meta Quest family, such as XR plugin selection and sideloading. By the end of these screens you will be able to produce a signed APK, install it on a device, troubleshoot common install errors, and capture logs to diagnose crashes. As you learn, pay attention to the keystore responsibilities and the common misstep of forgetting USB debugging; those two issues cause the most deployment friction. Think about one app you would like to test on a phone or headset — we'll use that as our running example throughout the lesson.

screens.title: Prepare the Android device for development
screens.subtitle: Enable Developer Options and USB Debugging to allow adb connections

narration.text: Preparing the Android device is the first essential step and a frequent source of frustration when it is missed. To enable Developer Options, open Settings, go to About phone, and tap the build number seven times. This unlocks Developer Options in Settings > System > Developer options. Within Developer Options, toggle on USB Debugging. This gives your computer the permission to install APKs and access device logs. Practically, if adb devices returns no entries, the most likely cause is USB Debugging being off or a faulty cable or driver on the computer. Remember to accept the RSA key prompt on the phone the first time you connect; without that confirmation adb will not list the device. A common misconception is that a device only needs to be 'visible' as storage for installation; Android requires USB Debugging for adb-based installs and log access. As an example, if you connect a phone and run adb devices and see an empty list, check that Developer Options exists, USB Debugging is enabled, and try a different USB mode or cable. Also verify any required drivers are installed on your development machine. Key takeaway: enabling Developer Options and USB Debugging is quick, but it must be done before Unity or adb can deploy and debug your app.

keyIdea.title: Device readiness
keyIdea.text: Enable Developer Options and USB Debugging and accept the device RSA prompt so adb can connect for install and debug.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Prepare Device
Process

Enable Developer Options & USB Debugging

Follow a small sequence to make your device accessible to adb and Unity.

  1. 1. Go to Settings > About phone and tap Build number seven times to enable Developer Options.
  2. 2. Open Settings > System > Developer options and toggle on USB debugging.
  3. 3. Connect device via USB, accept the computer's RSA key when prompted on the device.
  4. 4. Verify with adb devices.
Key Takeaway

If adb does not list your device, USB Debugging or the RSA confirmation is usually the issue. Check cable and drivers next.

Common Mistake
Treating a phone as USB storage is not enough. adb requires explicit developer access via USB Debugging and an accepted RSA key.
Quick check
adb devices
# Expected: a device id and 'device' state listed
Pro tip
If your device appears as 'unauthorized' in adb, unlock the phone and accept the RSA fingerprint popup.

screens.title: Unity Build Settings and XR Plug-in Management
screens.subtitle: Select Android platform and configure ARCore or VR plugins for target hardware

narration.text: Before building, ensure Unity is targeting Android and that your XR plug-ins are configured for the experience you need. In Build Settings choose Android and verify the scenes you want included are checked. In Project Settings open XR Plug-in Management and enable ARCore for AR projects or Oculus/OpenXR for VR headsets like Meta Quest. These plugins control runtime subsystems and influence Player Settings. For example, VR target devices may require a specific minimum A P I level and recommended color space settings; the chapter suggests choosing Linear color space for better visual quality on some Oculus configurations. A common misconception is that Unity will automatically select the correct XR plugin; you must enable and configure the plugin you intend to use. Also confirm Player Settings such as the Minimum A P I Level and package name are correct before building. If you plan to test on Quest, set the plugin target appropriately in the Oculus XR Plugin settings. These selections affect not only runtime compatibility but also what files and permissions are included in the final APK, so review them carefully before starting the build.

keyIdea.title: Correct platform & plugin
keyIdea.text: Select Android platform and enable the correct XR plugin (ARCore, Oculus, or OpenXR) to ensure runtime compatibility.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Build Settings
Definition

Platform & XR Plugin Selection

Choose Android in Build Settings and enable the correct XR plugins in Project Settings to match your target device.

Scenes
Ensure the scenes you want in the build are checked in File > Build Settings.
XR Plug-in Management
Enable ARCore for AR, or Oculus/OpenXR for VR. These control runtime subsystems and device integration.
Player Settings
Confirm package name, Minimum API Level, and recommended color space for your target headset.
Common Mistake
Leaving the wrong XR plugin enabled can cause missing runtime subsystems and errors when the app launches on the device.
Quick Checklist
  • Android selected in Build Settings
  • Correct scenes checked
  • ARCore or Oculus/OpenXR enabled in XR Plug-in Management
  • Player Settings: package name and Minimum API Level verified
Key Takeaway

XR plugin and Player Settings choices directly affect whether the APK will run on your target device; check them before building.

screens.title: Keystore and alias for signing
screens.subtitle: Why app signing matters and how to create a keystore in Unity

narration.text: Signing an Android app is mandatory; it proves the identity of the publisher and ensures future updates can be verified. In Unity this is handled in Edit > Project Settings > Player > Android tab > Publishing Settings where you'll find the Keystore Manager. If you don't already have a keystore you must create one, providing a secure password for the keystore file and then creating at least one alias or key inside it. Each alias has its own password and certificate details such as Name, Organization, City, and Country. Save the. keystore file in a safe location inside your project or a trusted backup. A major practical risk is losing the keystore or forgetting its password: you will not be able to publish updates to an app previously signed with that keystore. A common misconception is that you can recreate a keystore with the same name; cryptographic keys are unique, so losing access forces you to publish a new app with a new package name. Create strong passwords and store them securely. As an example workflow, create Project Keystore, add an alias like 'myarkey', fill the certificate fields, then select that keystore and alias before building your APK.

keyIdea.title: Digital identity
keyIdea.text: A keystore and alias digitally sign your APK. Protect them — losing them prevents updates to an existing app.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Keystore
Definition

Keystore & Alias

A keystore is a file containing cryptographic keys used to sign Android applications. An alias is a specific key inside that keystore for a particular app.

Create keystore
Open Keystore Manager in Unity's Player Publishing Settings, choose Create New, and select a secure location.
Create alias
Inside the keystore create a new key alias (example: myarkey) with its own password and certificate information.
Select for build
Choose your project keystore and alias before clicking Build so the APK is signed.
Security & Consequence

Use a strong password and back up the keystore file. If you lose it, you cannot sign updates for the same app identity on an app store.

Pro tip
Store the keystore outside your main project folder in a secure backup and document passwords in a password manager.
Key Takeaway

Keystore management is not optional. Treat the keystore and its passwords as the permanent identity of your app.

screens.title: Build: Build vs Build And Run & saving the APK
screens.subtitle: Choose the correct build flow and organize output files

narration.text: Unity offers two common build flows: Build and Build And Run. Build compiles the APK and saves it to disk, letting you inspect the file and install it manually. Build And Run compiles and then attempts to install and launch the app on a connected device immediately. For your first build, prefer Build so you can verify the APK location and keep a copy in a dedicated Builds/Android folder. This helps with version control and reproducible installs. Before building, confirm the scenes you need are checked in File > Build Settings. When Unity prompts for a save location, create a folder like Builds/Android and name your APK clearly, for example ARPlaneDetector. apk. If you later need to install manually with adb, you will navigate to that folder. A common mistake is overwriting previous builds without versioned filenames; this makes rollback or debugging harder. Also, building multiple times without changing the keystore or package name can produce confusing install errors if an older APK is still on the device. Keep folder organization simple and consistent so you always know where your last working APK is stored.

keyIdea.title: Controlled builds
keyIdea.text: Use Build to produce an APK you can archive. Reserve Build And Run for quick iterative checks when the device is ready.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Build Flow
Process

Build vs Build And Run

Decide if you want just an APK file or immediate deployment and launch on a connected device.

Build: Compiles APK and saves it to disk for manual installation and archiving.
Build And Run: Compiles and automatically installs on a connected device if adb recognizes it.
Best practice: Save builds to Builds/Android with versioned filenames like ARPlaneDetector_v1.apk.
Example

Create a folder 'Builds/Android' in your project root and save the first APK as ARPlaneDetector.apk. This keeps the output organized and makes manual adb installs straightforward.

Key Takeaway

Use Build for archival control and Build And Run for quick iteration when your device is prepped and recognized.

screens.title: Install APK using adb
screens.subtitle: Use adb commands to list devices and install APKs

narration.text: Once you have an APK file, use the Android Debug Bridge to install it onto a connected device. Start by connecting the device with USB and verifying the connection with adb devices. This should list your device id and state. If it does not, revisit Developer Options and USB Debugging. To install an APK from the folder where the file is saved, run the command adb install YourAppName. apk. If an older version exists and you want to replace it, you can either uninstall first with adb uninstall followed by your package name or use a replace option where appropriate. If adb reports installation errors, the error text usually indicates the cause — for example, INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE or INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS. A concrete example: navigate to Builds/Android and run adb install ARPlaneDetector. apk. After installation, locate and run the app on the device to verify AR features work. Remember to keep the package name consistent in Player Settings. This command-driven workflow is the most reliable way to get your build onto a device during development. Install APK using adb means use adb devices to verify connection and adb install to place the apk on the device for testing.. In practical terms, use adb commands to list devices and install apks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: adb install
keyIdea.text: Use adb devices to verify connection and adb install to place the APK on the device for testing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › adb Install
Commands
adb devices
adb install ARPlaneDetector.apk
adb uninstall com.yourcompany.yourapp
Navigate to your Builds/Android folder in the terminal before running adb install so the command finds your APK immediately.
Example
cd path/to/project/Builds/Android then run the install command for ARPlaneDetector.apk. If install fails because the app already exists, run adb uninstall with the package name and try again.
Common Mistake
Running adb install from a different folder will fail to find the APK. Always confirm your working directory or provide a full path to the apk file.
Key Takeaway

adb install is the reliable, scriptable way to sideload builds during development. Know the folder and package name.

screens.title: Common adb installation errors and fixes
screens.subtitle: Diagnose INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS, INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE, and device connection errors

narration.text: When installing APKs you will encounter a small set of recurring adb errors. INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS means the device already has an app with the same package name installed. The fix is to uninstall the existing package with adb uninstall com. yourcompany. yourapp and then run adb install again. INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE indicates the device lacks free space; free up storage or uninstall large apps before retrying. If adb reports device not found or an empty adb devices list, the cause is typically USB Debugging not enabled or an unaccepted RSA key prompt on the device. Another frequent misunderstanding is blaming the APK: many install failures are environmental rather than corrupt APK content. Always read the adb error message — it points directly to the type of problem. For persistent install issues on headsets, double-check the target A P I level and plugin compatibility. A useful habit is to run adb devices, then adb install, and if installation fails, immediately run adb logcat to capture detailed failure logs for Unity and ActivityManager. This sequence reveals whether the failure is permission, storage, or signature related.

keyIdea.title: Read the error
keyIdea.text: Error messages guide the fix: uninstall if already exists, free storage for insufficient space, and enable USB Debugging for connection issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Troubleshooting

Error: INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS

Cause: Package already present on device. Fix: adb uninstall <package.name> then adb install again.

Error: INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE

Cause: Not enough free storage on the device. Fix: free storage or uninstall large apps before reinstalling.

Error: device not found / empty adb list

Cause: USB Debugging off or RSA key not accepted. Fix: enable USB Debugging and accept the computer's RSA prompt on the device.

Check

If errors persist, use adb logcat to capture logs for Unity and ActivityManager to reveal deeper causes.

screens.title: Using adb logcat for on-device debugging
screens.subtitle: Capture filtered logs for Unity and ActivityManager to investigate crashes and runtime errors

narration.text: On-device debugging is vital because many issues only appear on hardware. adb logcat streams system and app logs in real time. The chapter recommends filtering to Unity and ActivityManager to reduce noise: adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager. This command shows Unity messages and the Android activity manager, which often logs app start failures, permissions problems, or exceptions. When diagnosing a crash at startup, run this command before launching the app so you capture the sequence from process creation onward. One misconception is to look only at Unity Editor console logs; those are different from the device logs and won't show device-specific errors. For prolonged investigation, redirect logcat to a file and inspect it after reproducing the issue. Example workflow: connect device, run adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager, then launch your installed app and watch for stack traces or explicit error messages. If you see a permission exception or an OpenXR failure, that points you to Player Settings or plugin configuration rather than asset issues. The final step is using these logs to decide whether to change settings, update the keystore, or adjust the build.

keyIdea.title: Live device logs
keyIdea.text: Use adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager to capture focused runtime logs that help pinpoint startup crashes and runtime exceptions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › adb logcat
Command
adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager
# Streams Unity and ActivityManager logs for focused troubleshooting
Start logcat before launching the app to capture the full startup trace. Save logs to a file if you need to analyze them later.
Example diagnostic flow
  1. 1. Connect device and run adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager.
  2. 2. Launch the app on the device.
  3. 3. Observe exceptions or errors in the log to identify the faulty subsystem.
Misconception

Device logs are not identical to Editor logs. Trust logcat for device-specific failures.

screens.title: Meta Quest and Android-based VR specifics
screens.subtitle: XR plugin choices, target API level, and sideloading considerations

narration.text: Building for Android-based VR headsets like Meta Quest follows the same APK flow, but there are platform-specific details to check. Use the Oculus XR Plugin or OpenXR plugin in XR Plug-in Management, and ensure the Minimum A P I Level aligns with the headset OS. For better visual fidelity on some Oculus devices the chapter suggests setting Color Space to Linear. Sideloading to Meta Quest is usually done with adb or with a specialized tool such as SideQuest for convenience; both methods install the APK directly onto the headset. When targeting Quest, confirm the plugin settings target the correct device and check any recommended Player Settings exposed by the plugin. A common pitfall is neglecting to set an appropriate Minimum A P I Level or leaving the wrong plugin active, which can prevent the app from launching on the headset. Also, remember that headsets may report different performance characteristics than phones; an experience that works on a phone may need optimization to run smoothly on Quest. When sideloading, follow the same adb install and adb logcat workflows to install and debug the application on the headset.

keyIdea.title: VR build differences
keyIdea.text: Select the proper XR plugin and target API level for Quest, and sideload via adb or SideQuest while testing performance on device.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › VR Targeting
Checklist
  • Enable Oculus or OpenXR in XR Plug-in Management.
  • Set Minimum API Level appropriate for the headset OS.
  • Consider Linear color space for improved visuals on some headsets.
Sideloading
Use adb install or SideQuest to sideload development builds onto Quest. Use adb logcat to capture headset logs.
Performance note
Headsets often need further optimization compared to phones. Test frame rate and CPU/GPU load with the Unity Profiler connected remotely.
Key Takeaway

Treat VR builds as a special target: plugin, API level, and performance checks matter for a successful headset deployment.

screens.title: On-device testing and profiling
screens.subtitle: Use Unity Profiler and runtime checks to validate behavior and performance

narration.text: Testing on device is not optional for AR and VR: sensors, performance, and platform integrations behave differently than in the Editor. After installing the APK, launch your app and exercise common interactions like plane detection for AR or controller tracking for VR. Monitor performance — dropped frames or tracking glitches indicate the need to profile and optimize. Unity's remote profiler can connect to a running device to capture C P U, G P U, and memory metrics. The chapter notes that these workflows are covered in a later chapter, but the practical rule is simple: always validate features and performance on the actual hardware. A misconception is assuming Editor play mode performance equals device performance; this is seldom true. As a concrete action, run a 60-second scenario of your app while profiling to capture hotspots. Use adb logcat in parallel to capture any runtime exceptions. The final goal is a stable, responsive experience on the target device, not merely a working scene in the Editor. On-device testing and profiling means profile and verify feature behavior on device; editor results often differ from real-world performance and tracking.. In practical terms, use unity profiler and runtime checks to validate behavior and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test on real hardware
keyIdea.text: Profile and verify feature behavior on device; Editor results often differ from real-world performance and tracking.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › On-Device Testing
Test Routine
  1. Install and launch the app on the device.
  2. Run through core scenarios for 60 seconds (plane detection, placement, interaction).
  3. Record performance via Unity Profiler connected remotely.
Diagnostics
Use adb logcat to capture runtime exceptions while the profiler shows CPU and memory pressure. Together they expose where to optimize.
Key Takeaway

A build that runs in the Editor may still perform poorly on device. Always profile and test on the target hardware.

screens.title: Activity: Build and Sideload an ARCore APK
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step guided activity to create keystore, build, and install using adb

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties together the chapter steps. Start with prerequisites: your Unity AR project configured for ARCore and a device with Developer Options and USB Debugging enabled. In Unity open Publishing Settings and create a keystore if needed. Create a new alias with certificate details and keep the keystore file and passwords secure. Next, open File > Build Settings, choose Android, ensure your AR scene(s) are checked, and click Build. Save the APK to Builds/Android with a clear name like ARPlaneDetector. apk. After the build completes, connect your device with USB and verify with adb devices. If the device appears, run adb install ARPlaneDetector. apk from that folder. If adb reports INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS, run adb uninstall com. yourcompany. yourapp and retry the install. Finally, launch the app on the device and verify plane detection and placement features. If the app crashes at startup, run adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager while launching to capture errors. Expected outcome: a signed APK installed on your device with AR features functioning. This activity reinforces keystore creation, build hygiene, and adb install and log workflows.

keyIdea.title: Practical build lab
keyIdea.text: Create a keystore, build an APK, sideload it with adb, and verify AR functionality on the device.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Activity

Build and Sideload an ARCore APK

Follow these steps in order to complete the lab successfully.

Step 1
Enable Developer Options and USB Debugging on your phone.
Step 2
Create a keystore and alias in Unity's Publishing Settings.
Step 3
Build the APK and save it to Builds/Android as ARPlaneDetector.apk.
Step 4
Connect device and verify with adb devices, then run adb install.
Step 5
If install fails, use adb uninstall com.yourcompany.yourapp and retry.
Step 6
Run adb logcat -s Unity ActivityManager if the app crashes to capture logs for diagnosis.
Expected Outcome

A signed APK installed on your phone that launches and performs AR plane detection and placement as in the Editor.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Commands & Tools
adb devices
Lists connected devices so you can confirm adb connectivity.
adb install
Installs an APK file onto the connected device for testing.

Streams device logs; filter for Unity and ActivityManager to diagnose errors.
